stem: A client taking chronic metoprolol succinate for hypertension and stable angina says, "My blood pressure is controlled, so I want to stop it today." Which teaching is most important?

options.A: Stop metoprolol today and monitor blood pressure at home, because controlled blood pressure indicates that chronic beta-blocker therapy can be ended without tapering.
options.B: Do not stop metoprolol abruptly; when discontinuation is planned, the dose is generally reduced gradually over 1 to 2 weeks with monitoring because sudden withdrawal can worsen myocardial ischemia.
options.C: Take metoprolol every other day for 48 hours and then stop, because a brief reduction period is sufficient to prevent withdrawal-related angina or myocardial infarction.
options.D: Replace metoprolol with a stimulant medication before stopping it, because the main withdrawal concern is persistent bradycardia and fatigue rather than recurrent ischemia.

rationale: Current DailyMed labeling warns that abrupt cessation of chronic beta-blocker therapy can exacerbate angina and has been associated with myocardial infarction. When discontinuing chronically administered metoprolol succinate, especially in ischemic heart disease, the dose should be reduced gradually over 1 to 2 weeks with monitoring. Patients should be warned not to interrupt therapy without clinician advice. Therefore B is correct. A recommends abrupt cessation. C uses an inadequate unsupported taper. D misstates the withdrawal risk and proposes an unsupported substitute.
educational_objective: Teach clients receiving chronic metoprolol not to stop it abruptly; planned discontinuation generally requires gradual dose reduction over 1 to 2 weeks with monitoring to reduce ischemic risk.
source_organization: DailyMed / U.S. National Library of Medicine
source_document_title: Metoprolol Succinate Extended-Release Tablets — Prescribing Information
source_version_date: Current DailyMed labeling; page current June 2026
source_locator: Warnings and Precautions 5.1 Abrupt Cessation of Therapy: abrupt cessation of certain beta-blockers has caused exacerbation of angina and, in some cases, myocardial infarction; when discontinuing chronically administered metoprolol succinate, particularly in ischemic heart disease, gradually reduce dosage over 1 to 2 weeks and monitor; warn patients not to interrupt therapy without physician advice.
source_claim_supported: Chronic metoprolol should not be stopped abruptly; taper over 1 to 2 weeks with monitoring because sudden withdrawal can worsen angina or precipitate myocardial infarction.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, printed pp. 38–41: provide medication education, evaluate medication response, identify adverse effects and risks, and safely manage medication changes.
blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — beta-blocker discontinuation teaching
correction_summary: Rebuilt all options to remove absolute-word cueing and use realistic but incorrect discontinuation strategies involving immediate cessation, an inadequately short taper, and an unsupported substitute medication.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Beta-blocker therapy — safe discontinuation of chronic metoprolol
audit_findings.stem: PASS — provides chronic therapy, controlled hypertension, and stable angina, directly activating the labeled abrupt-withdrawal risk.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS as distractor — controlled blood pressure does not make abrupt discontinuation safe.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS — directly matches the current labeling for gradual 1-to-2-week tapering and monitoring; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — a 48-hour alternate-day taper is not the labeled 1-to-2-week gradual reduction strategy.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — stimulant substitution is unsupported and the principal withdrawal concern includes recurrent myocardial ischemia.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — B is the only option that follows the explicit duration and monitoring recommendation without an unsafe workaround.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — A stops abruptly, C uses an insufficient taper, and D misstates the risk and adds an unsupported medication.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — no distractor uses the previous absolute-word pattern and all choices are clinically plausible medication-teaching statements.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies directly includes medication education and safe management of medication therapy.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether controlled blood pressure or stable angina could justify immediate cessation; current labeling explicitly warns against abrupt discontinuation even in patients treated only for hypertension because coronary disease may be unrecognized, leaving B uniquely correct.
